stem: A client receiving oral cancer therapy tells the nurse, 'Even with insurance, the copay is so high that I have been skipping some doses to make the prescription last longer.' Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Recognize possible financial toxicity, assess how treatment costs are affecting adherence and basic needs, and connect the client with the oncology team's financial or social-support resources while notifying the prescribing team about the missed doses.
options.B: Explain that financial toxicity applies only to clients without health insurance, so the main issue is medication noncompliance.
options.C: Tell the client to continue reducing doses independently until finances improve because some treatment is better than none.
options.D: Avoid discussing costs because financial concerns are separate from clinical cancer care and should not influence the nursing plan.

rationale: NCI defines financial toxicity as problems related to the cost of medical care and notes that it can occur even in people who have health insurance because of copayments, deductibles, coinsurance, treatment-related work loss, and other expenses. Financial toxicity can affect access, quality of life, and treatment adherence; patients may skip doses, take less medication, or not fill prescriptions to save money. The nurse should therefore assess the cost-related barrier, notify the treatment team about missed therapy, and coordinate available financial/social resources rather than labeling the issue as simple noncompliance or endorsing independent dose reduction.
educational_objective: Recognize cost-related medication underuse as a manifestation of financial toxicity and coordinate assessment, treatment-team communication, and financial/social support to protect adherence and client well-being.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Financial Toxicity (Financial Distress) and Cancer Treatment (PDQ®)–Patient Version; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — Financial Toxicity
source_version_date: Current NCI PDQ and dictionary resources accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: PDQ — General Information About Financial Toxicity; insurance-related risk; Effects of Financial Toxicity, including medication adherence and quality of life; NCI Dictionary — 'financial toxicity'
source_claim_supported: NCI defines financial toxicity as cost-related financial problems that may occur even with health insurance and may reduce access and quality of life. NCI documents behaviors such as skipping doses, taking less medication, or not filling prescriptions because of cost.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care — resource utilization, continuity/coordination of care, interdisciplinary referral, barriers to care, and client-centered planning
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — financial barriers to cancer treatment adherence and coordination of support resources
correction_summary: Rebuilt the original financial-toxicity definition item into an applied medication-adherence and resource-coordination scenario. Replaced generic ASCO sourcing with NCI PDQ and NCI terminology, explicitly included an insured client to eliminate the misconception that only uninsured clients experience financial toxicity, and required the nurse to assess cost-related barriers, communicate missed doses, and coordinate support rather than merely identify the term.
audit_findings: Original item tested terminology with weak distractors rather than requiring recognition of a clinically meaningful barrier and nursing response.
NCI directly supports that financial toxicity can occur despite insurance and can lead to skipped doses, lower medication use, reduced access, and lower quality of life.
The final item does not endorse independent dose reduction and requires communication with the prescribing team when doses have already been missed.
Resource coordination is kept general rather than promising a specific financial program or coverage outcome that may vary by institution or insurer.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, stigmatizing noncompliance framing, or unresolved source conflict.
